title: The nasal dots
hookLine: two marks, one hum: why does Gurmukhi keep both the tippi and the bindi?
tomorrow: why do some copies have no spaces between the words?

cards: One period after ok, and a friend texts back: are you mad? The letters didn't change. A dot did.

Gurmukhi has small marks of its own riding above the letters, and they come with a puzzle. Take sangat, the gathering of people around the Guru's words. Over its first letter sits a tiny curved mark: a tippi.
Now take maan, the word for mother. The same kind of hum through the nose, but this time the mark is a single dot: a bindi. Two marks, doing what sounds like one job.
Why would a script keep both?

teach.b: Here's the answer. The tippi and the bindi both add a nasal sound, the hum of the n in sangat.

teach.h: THE VOWEL SIGN PICKS THE MARK.
teach.b: Which one a word takes depends on its neighbor, the vowel sign on that letter. In the rule learners are taught, a long aa, as in maan, takes the bindi. A plain letter with its quiet a, as in sangat, takes the tippi.
There's a third mark in the family: the addhak, a small curve that tells you to double the next letter and lean on it. Now the part worth repeating tonight.
The word Granth itself, in Gurmukhi, carries a tippi. Take it off, and the book's own name loses its n.
Drop the tippi from sangat and you're left with sagat, which isn't the word at all: the gathering vanishes with one missing mark.

So small marks matter isn't fussiness. Someone reading aloud in a gurdwara, or at a kitchen table for a grandparent, is carrying the sound to people who trust it. The marks are how a reader keeps that trust.
They're tiny on the page and large in the ear.

how: Learners of Gurmukhi are taught the tippi, the bindi and the addhak along with the vowel signs, and readers of Gurbani take care to sound the nasal marks so each word is heard as it is written.

games.q: a friend learning Gurmukhi shrugs: tippi or bindi, who cares, they both add an n. she's writing maan, mother. what do you tell her?
o: she's right: either mark works, and a reader will figure out the word.
she's wrong: the two marks make different sounds, so maan would change meaning.
same hum, but the vowel sign picks the mark: a long aa, as in maan, takes the bindi.
games.why: the tippi and the bindi share a sound and split the work by vowel sign. maan, with its long aa, takes the bindi; sangat, with a plain letter, takes the tippi.

practice: Open a gutka, a steek or a Gurbani app to any page and hunt for one tippi or one bindi.

When you find it, rest your eyes on it and say the word softly twice: once with the hum, once without, and hear what the small mark was holding up. Then breathe slowly, and let the hum fade on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Tippi: a small curved mark above a Gurmukhi letter that adds a nasal hum, the n in sangat and in Granth. The fourth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: tippi, the mark that adds a nasal hum. Its own spelling uses an addhak to double the p.

carryVoice: Keep this: small marks matter, and one of them can hold up a whole word. Four of twenty.
